article_text:
“ Tokyo in 33 RPM ,” a feature documentary about the jazz scene in Japan’s capital, is in the works from director Tanmay Srivastava and Synergy Pictures U.K.

The project will be presented at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market that runs alongside the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

The film moves between Tokyo’s working musicians, the people who run its jazz kissa – cafés built around listening to vinyl – and collectors who have chronicled the music for decades. It traces how jazz took root in Japan and how a new generation is reshaping it.

On camera are bassist Hino Kenji, known as Jino, whose father is trumpeter Hino Terumasa, the country’s best-known player of the instrument; Lucas Minoru Poulshock, a musician who goes by Mino and also hosts an Apple Music podcast and runs a listening bar; and historian and record collector Hori Toru. The crew also drops in on Masako, a Shimokitazawa jazz café now in the hands of a third generation, and on No Room for Squares, which Nakata Kohei founded. Gentle Forest Jazz Band and GCR Orchestra also appear.

“Tokyo is a city that never really slows down, but you can step into a small room where everyone has come for one reason: to listen,” said Srivastava. “Outside those rooms, you meet musicians taking jazz in completely new directions. I wanted this film to bring both worlds together. That’s the Tokyo I found most interesting.”

A first round of filming in Japan has already been completed, and the team has put together a short-form version from that material. A teaser is also out. Production will return to Tokyo April 1–22, 2027, for the final shoot, with completion targeted for June that year.

Srivastava produces alongside Sky Cheema and Jackson McKeever, with Poulshock, Paul Adrian and Jade Kurian as executive producers. Synergy Pictures U.K. and Double Drama Productions are the production companies. McKeever’s Lucky 18 is on board as production partner, while Latakoo, a technology company based in Austin, Texas, is production and technology partner.

U.K. producer Cheema said viewers don’t need any background in jazz to connect with the people in the film. “Some have spent their lives playing the music. Others have built places where people can hear it properly. What matters is how much of themselves they’ve put into it. That’s what we want audiences to come away with.”

The team is readying the feature for a possible international festival bow in 2027.

For now, the focus is April, when the cameras head back to Tokyo.

Shows

The Alien in the Archive: Tony Albert at the MCA Australia

TONY ALBERT ,

Story, Place , 2023, appropriated found objects, 200 x 400 cm. Photo by Rhett Hammerton. Courtesy the artist and the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia, Sydney.

Tony Albert Not a Souvenir Museum of Contemporary Art Australia Sydney May 21–Oct 19, 2026

At Tallawoladah, the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA) sits between two economies of Australian culture: the institutional archive and the souvenir trade. Located near the foundational site of British colonization and amid the tourist precincts of Circular Quay and The Rocks, it was a particularly charged setting for “Tony Albert: Not a Souvenir,” the Girramay, Yidinji, and Kuku Yalanji artist’s largest exhibition to date. Bringing together more than 150 works, the show examined how Aboriginal culture has been simplified, commodified, and circulated—and how these representations might be reclaimed.

“Clarity,” Wierdi curator Bruce Johnson McLean emphasized, guided the exhibition’s development. Yet clarity is complicated when confronting material at once familiar and insidious. Central to Albert’s practice is Aboriginalia: objects made largely by non-Indigenous people for non-Indigenous audiences, depicting Aboriginal people, art, and culture. More than 2,500 examples from the artist’s personal collection were presented, including matchboxes, ashtrays, tea towels, figurines, plates, and velvet paintings.

TONY ALBERT ’s “Not a Souvenir” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA), Sydney, 2026. Photo by Ravyna Jassani. Courtesy the artist and MCA.

TONY ALBERT ’s

Brothers (The Prodigal Son) I , 2020, glass, lead, photographic decal, steel 180 x 60 cm (left); and

Optimism II , 2026, pigment print on paper, each 100 x 100 cm (right), at “Not a Souvenir,” the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA), Sydney, 2026. Photo by Jessica Maurer. Courtesy the artist and MCA.

In the opening room, curated by former MCA curator of First Nations art Rebecca Ray, these objects formed an overflowing yet calculated taxonomy. Displayed en masse, their sheer volume revealed the scale at which racist imagery has been reproduced and consumed, demanding sustained attention to material commonly dismissed as kitsch. Albert and Johnson McLean describe this archive as “anecdotal, not academic,” grounded in the artist’s sustained proximity with the objects rather than institutional classification. Its entry into MCA exposed the exclusions underpinning the museum’s categories of cultural value.

The next room shifted from caricatured Aboriginal bodies to contemporary Indigenous figures. Created with Girramay artist Erica Muriata, Albert’s photographic series Optimism II (2026) depicts Indigenous people around Sydney Harbour carrying jarwun —traditional baskets woven by Muriata—filled with present-day ephemera such as headphones, native plants, water bottles, and koala trinkets. Photographed from behind, the figures look across the water; viewers share their horizon rather than inspect them as anthropological subjects. The work reclaims the shoreline; the Aboriginal body is no longer the keepsake.

This direct visual address also responds to MCA’s institutional setting and foot traffic, where international tourists make up a substantial portion of visitors. The exhibition does not presume familiarity with Albert’s practice or the domestic trade in Aboriginalia. But accessibility does not slip into simplification. As Johnson McLean observes, the commercial mechanisms of racial souvenir trade are hardly unique to Australia; Albert uses local ephemera to expose a broader global colonial logic that any viewer can readily recognize.

TONY ALBERT ’s

Disconnected , 2025, synthetic polymer paint and found objects applied to timber, at “Not a Souvenir,” the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA), Sydney, 2026. Photo by Ravyna Jassani. Copyright and courtesy the artist and MCA.

Language remains one of his sharpest critical tools. Disconnected (2025) is a wall-text manifesto composed of 450 letters cast from fragments of broken Aboriginalia. The work names the violence enacted by the very commodities from which it is made. Rather than discarding detritus, Albert splinters and reassembles it into a architectural counter-narrative, transforming the physical material of objectification into an apparatus of Indigenous critique.

This strategy extends to the institutional canon of Australian art. Renowned 20th-century painter Margaret Preston sought to establish a national modernist idiom partly through appropriating Aboriginal iconography, frequently without acknowledging makers or cultural restrictions. Albert’s Conversations with Margaret Preston: Christmas Bells (2021), based on Preston’s 1925 woodcut, is pieced together from vintage fabric squares and commercial tea towels emblazoned with the generic label “Australian Aboriginal Art.” Neither homage nor repudiation, the work forces the formal appeal of Preston’s print to share space with its exploitative legacy. Albert suspends the viewer within this contradiction, allowing beauty and violence, dry wit and critique, to co-exist as unresolved conditions of Australian culture and history.

Installation views of TONY ALBERT ’s “Not a Souvenir” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Australia (MCA), Sydney, 2026. Photos by Jessica Maurer (left) and Ravyna Jassani (right). Courtesy the artist and MCA.

Conversation operates not only as Albert’s subject but as his primary methodology. The exhibition emerges from a 25-year dialogue with Johnson McLean alongside a longstanding practice of working collaboratively with artists, communities, and institutions. These relationships allow him to challenge the limits of what the museum collects, validates, and exhibits, while remaining within its institutional machinery. As Johnson McLean puts it, “the relationship is the project; the work is the product.”

The exhibition’s public initiative, the Aboriginalia Appeal, expands this relational framework by inviting visitors to donate objects they no longer feel comfortable owning. Albert treats the acquisition of these objects as restorative and even “therapeutic,” as it converts domestic kitsch into material evidence of how mainstream Australia has codified Indigenous people. Albert neither demands that the museum sanitize Aboriginalia nor asks the archive to purge on cue. Instead, he makes each answer for the other. At Tallawoladah, where colonial history, cultural authority, and tourist commerce remain uneasily entwined, he transforms the souvenir from a stagnant trope to active testimony within a living, contested history.

Michelle Wang is a writer exploring culture, art, film, and pop culture based in Sydney and London.

Source: Berlinale

‘David Bowie “Stage”’

Brett Morgen’s David Bowie “ Stage” will have its world premiere at the 77 th Berlin Film Festival (February 10-21, 2027).

The film features previously unseen concert footage of Bowie from his 1978 Isolar II World Tour, in support of his landmark Heroes album. Using a three-screen presentation, transparent LED screens and large-scale projections, it is described as an “immersive and sound light experience”.

David Bowie “Stage” is the first title announced for Berlin and will premiere at the festival on February 14.

Morgen previously directed the Bafta-nominated documentary Moonage Daydream which followed Bowie’s rise to fame and had its world premiere at Cannes Film Festival in 2022.

The director will also participate in the European Film Market’s talks programme, with further details to be announced in the coming weeks.

David Bowie “Stage” is a collaboration between Morgen, Rob Hallett’s Wonderworld and the David Bowie Estate.

article_text:
One of Batman’s creepiest villains is descending upon the box office this weekend.

Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “ Clayface ” made $3.5 million in Thursday previews at the box office, and it’ll face some tough competition from the buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary “ You Can See Everything ” from A24.

“Clayface” is projected to make $25 million to $35 million in its opening weekend, though some rival estimates put it lower at $22 million to $28 million. The R-rated comic book movie cost just $44 million to produce, much lower than fellow DC movies like “Superman” and “Supergirl,” so it should be easy to turn a profit. It’s on track to add $20 million to $25 million overseas for a global opening of $45 million to $55 million. Directed by James Watkins, “Clayface” follows the shape-shifting Batman foe, who starts out as a Hollywood actor who undergoes a dangerous medical procedure that goes horribly wrong.

The directors filmed Theranos CEO Holmes ahead of her 11-year prison sentence, and the movie has been building hype and Oscar buzz in the last few weeks.

As “Clayface” and “You Can See Everything” battle for first place, they’ll both prevail over several fellow new releases this weekend. Black Bear’s rom-com “ Wicker ,” starring Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård, made $620,000 in Thursday previews and is expected to make $6 million to $8 million by Sunday. Laika’s stop-motion animated movie “Wildwood” is aiming for a debut in the same range. Sony and director Taika Waititi’s “Klara and the Sun,” starring Jenna Ortega, is expected to make just $2 million. 風を継ぐもの はじまり

劇場公開日： 2026年11月13日

解説・あらすじ

激動の幕末に生きた新選組の若者たちの青春を新解釈で描くオリジナルテレビアニメ「風を継ぐもの」を、2027年1月の放送に先駆け、劇場先行版としてスクリーン上映。劇場先行版では、記憶喪失の主人公・立川迅助と壬生浪士組の仲間たちとの出会いや、局長筆頭・芹沢鴨とのエピソードを上映する。 文久3年6月。京都・壬生浪士組屯所に、記憶をなくした隊士の青年が運び込まれる。青年は副長助勤・沖田総司から、自分が「立川迅助」という人物であることを教えられ、隊士としての日々を過ごすようになる。新選組は幕末の混迷のなかで次第に存在感を増し、迅助たちは激動の波に飲み込まれていく。やがて迅助がすべての記憶を取り戻したとき、世界は大きな変貌を遂げる。 脚本は、演劇集団キャラメルボックスの創設者のひとりで、同じく新選組を題材にした舞台「風を継ぐ者」をはじめとする「立川迅助シリーズ」でも知られる劇作家・成井豊。「GAMBA ガンバと仲間たち」の河村友宏が、Live2Dとセルアニメーションを融合させた新しい映像表現に挑み、ロックバンド「くるり」の岸田繁が初めてテレビアニメの劇伴を担当。アイドルグループ「Snow Man」の佐久間大介が主人公・迅助の声を務め、声優としてテレビアニメ初主演を果たした。

“ We Had a Plan ,” a documentary about a gay Filipino couple who head home after a decade as undocumented cleaners in the Netherlands, has been picked up for international sales by Paris-based Cat&Docs ahead of its world premiere at IDFA .

Variety has the exclusive first look at the trailer.

Directed by Suzanne Raes and co-directed by Venice De Castro Atienza, the film will bow in the Luminous strand of the International Documentary Festival Amsterdam, which runs Nov. 12-22. It is also in the running for IDFA’s Best Dutch Film Award.

Related Stories

Jamie Dornan Says There's 'Pressure' to Taking Over Aragorn Role in 'Lord of the Rings: Hunt for Gollum': I'm Not 'Trying to Outdo' Viggo Mortensen

Paul and Daniel spent 10 years cleaning in the Netherlands without papers before moving back to the Philippines, where their relatives now regard them as rich. They arrive with big ideas for the life ahead of them. Money and optimism only go so far, though. As the savings from their years abroad run down, and the limits on their freedom as a gay couple close in, the relationship comes under strain.

“We shaped this film into a bittersweet love story about a couple whose relationship is tested by global inequalities in wealth, social security and acceptance of queer people,” Raes said. “It reveals the sacrifices migrant workers make to achieve their goals, humanizing an often invisible workforce.”

De Castro Atienza said that Paul and Daniel, after 12 years away with no way of going back, had gambled everything on a better future for themselves and their family. “As a Filipino filmmaker who has also left my home country, I approach their story with closeness and intimacy, recognizing the collective experience of choosing between leaving to provide for loved ones and staying to share a life with them. In ‘We Had a Plan,’ we witness two people try to change the configuration of the world to build a place for their love.”

Catherine Le Clef, president and CEO of Cat&Docs, said the company had responded straight away to the warmth of the film and its likable protagonists. “Through their personal stories, the film offers a deeply human perspective on a foreign workforce that is too often reduced to statistics, stereotypes or simply made invisible. It is also an important reminder of the very real human cost behind the systems that depend on their labor. We felt that this combination of intimacy, tenderness and social relevance made the film particularly powerful and timely.”

Raes’ earlier films include “Close to Vermeer” (2023) and “Where Dragons Live” (2024), the latter earning her a BAFTA Scotland nomination. De Castro Atienza’s first feature, “Last Days at Sea” (2021), debuted at the Berlinale and went on to Visions du Réel, Hot Docs and IDFA.

Ilja Roomans produced for Dutch outfit Docmakers, with Alemberg Ang co-producing for the Philippines’ Daluyong Studios. De Castro Atienza executive produced through Svemirko Film Productions. Cinema Delicatessen will handle distribution in the Netherlands.

article_text:
“Category fraud” is having a crossover moment.

It happens every year, in awards cycles for both film and television. Campaigners submit films, shows and individual performances in categories they have no business being in, like a drama masquerading as a comedy or a blatant leading role being tipped for a supporting category. Industry reactions to some of these bold decisions, however, feel louder this year.

Related Stories

This creative maneuvering with category submissions happens for a reason: to improve the perceived odds of winning a trophy. Yet increasingly, the misrepresentations are spilling into broader industry discourse. (Just Google the limited series “The Beast in Me,” which was greenlit for a second season and Emmy winner Matthew Rhys.)

This year, these so-called crimes seem to be targeting comedy categories. Curry Barker’s “ Obsession ,” made for $750,000 and now surpassing $500 million worldwide, was submitted by Focus Features as a musical or comedy for the Golden Globes , putting breakout star Inde Navarrette in the comedy actress race. Yes, there are laughs. But by and large, audiences were exposed to the horrors of a woman robbed of control over her own mind and body.

Not long after, Bleecker Street submitted Mike Leigh’s “ Tender Loving Care ” in the same comedy categories. Barely anyone blinked, perhaps because so few have seen it yet. The film features drunken sing-alongs and dancing with abandon in the family kitchen. It also features hospital visits and aging parents coming to terms with the final chapters of life. Hardly a laughing matter for anyone who has seen their loved ones slow down.

A chuckle does not equate to comedy. The strategists know it, and so do the Globes. What’s missing is the nerve to define it and, more importantly, enforce it. This dilemma isn’t new. A decade ago, Ridley Scott’s “The Martian” won the Golden Globe for best motion picture comedy. You know, the one about a man stranded on Mars, trying not to starve to death. LOL! Wonder if the Globes will remember that when Amazon MGM’s “Project Hail Mary” comes calling, with Ryan Gosling and an adorable alien rock each trying to save their civilizations.

Universal entered “Get Out” as a comedy in 2017 and got away with it. Focus tried it in 2020 with “Promising Young Woman,” about a woman avenging a friend’s assault. That time, voters said no and moved it to drama.

The current Globes rulebook states a movie “primarily intended to have a serious or dramatic tone” with “comedic overtones or elements” belongs in drama.

The Globes don’t account for intent, but they make all decisions using their “sole discretion” and their final rulings don’t come with an appeals process.

When a submission is called into question, a committee assembled by the Golden Globes reviews the case and rules on potential disputes, whether they involve genre classification or lead-versus-supporting campaigns. Some strategists, anticipating that the committee may raise flags, now try to get ahead of the process by submitting additional documentation, including filmmaker quotes and source materials, to explain why a film belongs in its intended category.

One top awards campaigner says that despite the attempts, the truth usually wins out.

“You have to be up front and honest with your filmmakers,” says one awards strategist. “It’s about what sets up the movie for success overall. And if you think both classifications are too competitive, ‘frauding’ your movie doesn’t make it easier. The opposite will happen.”

Musicals can be just as tricky to classify. “Ray” and “Walk the Line” competed in the Globes’ musical or comedy category. Still, in recent years, the organization has emphasized that songs must propel the story forward, rather than appear as performances, to qualify. That distinction sent “Bohemian Rhapsody” and “Elvis” to the drama category. By that standard, “Michael”’s classification remains an open question. Jaafar Jackson performs many of Michael Jackson’s biggest hits in the biopic, but whether those musical sequences are integral to the storytelling or simply re-creations of the King of Pop’s performances could determine where the film lands.

The Globes could revisit their rules, but any awards campaigner will tell you: There’s always a way to moonwalk around them.

"text": "在为这部电影进行调研的过程中，您有哪些经历？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：我的经历非常丰富多样，特别是在与面临这些问题的年轻女性及家属交谈时。有些人已经进入了修道院，有些人则没有；还有些人曾进入修道院，后来又退出了。在调研过程中，我不予置评。我更感兴趣的是人们的感受以及是什么在触动他们。在此基础上，我才塑造了电影中的人物。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "您对宗教机构的探访进展如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：我们与教会人士进行了交谈，其中包括神父和修女。由于明确了我们是抱着严肃认真的态度，我们得以在教堂里拍摄仪式和典礼。教会人士也接受了电影中存在与他们想法不同、不信教的角色。与心理学家的交谈对我也非常重要。由于我不信教，我是从人性的视角来讲述这个故事的。与心理学家探讨究竟是何种环境和关系会促使如此年轻的人产生如此强烈的宗教情感，是非常有意思的。因为当事人确实会感受到一种与爱情相似的强大情感。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "天主教绝对教会对这部电影有何反应？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：很好。天主教堂当初也曾对皮埃尔·保罗·帕索里尼的《马太福音》（Das 1. Evangelium - Matthäus）持正面态度。《信》以尊重对待所有角色，并试图理解他们。这部电影既没有取笑宗教人士，也没有嘲笑信仰的感觉。因此，我能理解天主教堂对该片持相当积极的态度。", "links": [{"text": "Das 1. "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：这就好比一场决斗，因为迈特极力克制自己。但她撞上了一堵墙，因为这些机构对理性的论证并不开放。迈特提出了合理的论据：这个女孩还很年轻。为什么我们不给她更多时间呢？然而，人们认为是上帝旨意的东西，是无法用理性论据去质疑的。这正是宽容往往变得如此艰难的原因。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "paragraph", "text": "你的所有电影都围绕着家庭展开。对你而言，家庭意味着什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：家庭是社会的细胞。当情感纽带运转良好、彼此以礼相待时，它可以成为避风港和极其美妙的地方。但通常情况并非如此。谈论这一点是一个巨大的禁忌。直到今天，与自己的家庭决裂仍被视为绝对禁忌——即便发生了痛苦的事情、某人在情感上遭到忽视或类似情形。我们受到的教育是不与家庭决裂，尽管有时这才是最健康的。我对家庭中这些令人不快的领域很感兴趣——既把它作为一种机构，也把它作为参照群体。有时，它是那个让你感到安全、被理解、对你一生影响最深的地方。但它也可能是让你遭受最大伤害的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的电影故事发生在室内：家庭住宅、修道院，还有学校。这种美学在多大程度上与故事相契合？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：最令人不快、最动摇人心或最紧张刺激的事情都发生在受保护的私人空间里——而这通常就是室内。正是在厨房里半掩着门进行的那些对话，或者是午餐桌上的那些讨论。宗教圣召这种非常个人的故事同样也发生在室内，发生在成年人与未成年人之间、在亲密氛围下的谈话中，谈论的则是朋友之类的事情。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在视觉上也同样非常有趣。我讲述的是一个女孩感受到过闭关修道院生活的召唤、并想要隐退到四面墙之中的故事。这其中也涉及封闭和幽闭恐惧症的概念。家庭同样也可能具有极强的幽闭恐惧症。我们希望将这两个空间彼此靠拢——宗教世界与家庭并非彼此隔绝。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmdienst.de/bild/filmdb/370848/glaube-szenenbild-1.jpg?t=1782310300", "alt": "避难所还是监狱？《信》所聚焦的室内空间依然保持着两面性", "caption": "避难所还是监狱？《信》所聚焦的室内空间依然保持着两面性（© MFA+/David Herranz）", "credit": "Filmdienst", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "音乐在电影中非常重要。创作过程是怎样的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏亚：我在使用音乐时非常克制。你很容易用它来施加巨大影响、操纵或过分突出某些方面。只有当音乐能够创造出额外的层面或对比时，它才让我感兴趣。在本片中，这个合唱团就是这样一个元素——艾纳拉正是在这项课外活动中结识了那个男孩和他的朋友们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "合唱团在另一方面也很有趣，因为合唱音乐本身就带有一种灵性。即便它不是宗教性的，也同样拥有某种超越性。在相对日常的场景中加入这种元素，感觉非常美妙。我的主角是一名青少年。她的独特之处在于，她感受到了一种同龄朋友们所感觉不到的超越性或灵性。对我而言，音乐是将这种感受传达给观众的一种方式。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "电影开场我用了一首盖维多的曲子，这位说唱歌手不仅在年轻人中很受欢迎。在圣塞巴斯蒂安的首映式上，音乐刚一响起观众就已经进入状态了；片头字幕还在播放时，大家就想鼓掌了。然而十字架突然出现，所有人都震惊了：“这到底讲的是什么？”好吧，讲的正是这两点：一个青少年，以及她拥有宗教圣召。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你在圣塞巴斯蒂安领取最佳影片奖时曾说，电影是交流与相遇的场所。你这话是什么意思？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "鲁伊斯·德·阿苏阿：我喜欢一部能引发我思考的电影，不仅是在理智层面，也触及情感。情感可以引发思考；电影始终也可以是一种对话的邀请。你和其它人坐在一起，在放映厅里共同经历一些事情。之后，你可能会产生一种交流的冲动，想去谈谈电影在你身上引发的触动。在《信仰》上映时，许多人走出影院，都带着强烈的倾诉欲来谈论这部电影。但重点不仅仅是与那些与你想法相似的人进行对话。直面不同的观点，同样是一种非常重要的能力。这是我们已经失去的东西。然而，这对于社会的交流与共处又是如此重要。", article_text:
Beim Filmfestival in San Sebastián wurde „ Glaube “ von Alauda Ruiz de Azúa mit der „Goldenen Muschel“ als bester Film geehrt. Am 29. Oktober kommt das Drama über die Entscheidung einer Jugendlichen, in ein Kloster einzutreten, und die Kontroversen, die dies auslöst, nun in die deutschen Kinos. Im Interview spricht die Regisseurin über die Rolle der katholischen Kirche, die Reaktionen auf ihren Film und warum Toleranz schwierig, aber notwendiger denn je ist.

Was war der Auslöser für Ihren Film?

Alauda Ruiz de Azúa: Die Geschichte habe ich lange mit mir herumgetragen: Noch während meines Studiums erzählte man mir, dass ein Mädchen aus Bilbao, das so alt wie ich war, eine religiöse Berufung verspürte und in ein Kloster eingetreten sei. Ich bin weder religiös noch gläubig. Doch mit Anfang zwanzig machte mich diese Geschichte neugierig, aber auch ratlos: Wie konnte eine so junge Frau plötzlich eine so radikale Entscheidung treffen? Viele Jahre später fand ich den richtigen Ansatzpunkt, um diese Geschichte zu erzählen. Wie geht eine Familie damit um? Mit dieser Perspektive und all den Konflikten, die daraus entstehen könnten, hatte ich den Film bereits klar vor Augen.

Das könnte Sie auch interessieren:

Weitere Interviews

Sie sind 1978 geboren, drei Jahre nach Francos Tod. Gehören Sie noch zu einer Generation, die vom Nationalkatholizismus beeinflusst wurde?

Ruiz de Azúa: Die Generation meiner Eltern hatte die Macht der Kirche während der Diktatur noch erlebt. Die Kirche war für die Bildung zuständig – und zwar auf eine sehr fragwürdige, autoritäre und aggressive Art und Weise. Es gab keine Alternative. Für meine Generation existierten hingegen schon zahlreiche Alternativen. Ich besuchte beispielsweise eine staatliche Schule, hatte aber auch Freundinnen, die auf kirchliche Schulen gingen.

Besitzt ein Film wie „Glaube“ in einem immer noch sehr katholischen Land wie Spanien einen kathartischen Effekt?

Ruiz de Azúa: Als plötzlich Menschen aus allen Altersgruppen und mit unterschiedlichen religiösen Überzeugungen über Glaubensfragen diskutierten und sich austauschen wollten, haben wir gemerkt, dass unser Film unbequemer war, als wir es selbst gedacht hatten. Er hat zu einem manchmal kontroversen, aber auch tiefgründigen Austausch über das Thema Glauben beigetragen.

In diesen Diskussionen gibt es interessanterweise nicht zwei Lager, sondern viele unterschiedliche Sichtweisen. Unabhängig davon, ob sie religiös sind oder nicht, nehmen manche Menschen den Film eher wörtlich. Für sie muss es einen Guten und einen Bösen geben, einen Gewinner und einen Verlierer. Andere hingegen können die Komplexität der Situation aushalten und den Fragen nach einer möglichen Indoktrination oder nach der Legalität solcher Entscheidungen sehr junger Menschen nachgehen.

Ist die Kirche noch ein polarisierender Faktor in der spanischen Gesellschaft?

Ruiz de Azúa: Die Kirche ist nach wie vor ein Thema, das polarisiert. In meinem Film geht es aber um mehr als Religion oder die katholische Kirche. Viele unserer aktuellen Konflikte haben mit Toleranz zu tun. In den sozialen Netzwerken sehe ich ständig, wie die Grenzen ausgetestet werden: Was können wir noch tolerieren und was nicht? Wie lange und bis zu welchem Punkt? Dabei spielt natürlich auch das Religiöse oder der Katholizismus eine Rolle.

Was haben Sie bei den Recherchen zu dem Film erlebt?

Ruiz de Azúa: Meine Erfahrungen waren sehr vielfältig, vor allem in den Gesprächen mit jungen Frauen und Familien, die vor diesen Themen standen. Einige waren ins Kloster eingetreten, andere nicht; wieder andere waren eingetreten und später wieder ausgetreten. Bei meinen Recherchen urteile ich nicht. Mich interessiert vielmehr, was die Menschen empfinden und was sie bewegt. Auf dieser Grundlage entwickle ich dann die Figuren für den Film.

Wie verliefen Ihre Erkundungen in den religiösen Institutionen?

Ruiz de Azúa: Wir haben mit Menschen aus der Kirche gesprochen, darunter Priestern und Ordensschwestern. Wir haben in Kirchen Rituale und Zeremonien drehen dürfen, weil klar war, dass wir das ernst nahmen. Die Kirchenleute haben auch akzeptiert, dass es im Film Figuren gibt, die anders denken als sie und nicht religiös sind. Wichtig waren für mich auch Gespräche mit Psychologen. Da ich nicht gläubig bin, habe ich den Film aus einer menschlichen Perspektive erzählt. Es war interessant, mit den Psychologen darüber zu sprechen, welche Umstände und Beziehungen bei einem so jungen Menschen solch starke religiöse Gefühle hervorrufen können. Denn die Betroffenen empfinden tatsächlich ein mächtiges Gefühl, das dem der Liebe ähnelt.

Wie waren die Reaktionen der katholischen Kirche auf den Film?

Ruiz de Azúa: Gut. Die katholische Kirche hatte ja auch „ Das 1. Evangelium - Matthäus “ von Pier Paolo Pasolini positiv begrüßt. „Glaube“ behandelt alle Figuren mit Respekt und versucht, sie zu verstehen. Der Film macht sich weder über religiöse Menschen noch über das Gefühl des Glaubens lustig. Daher verstehe ich, dass die katholische Kirche dem Film durchaus positiv gegenübersteht.

Was ist „Las Betinas“ für ein Orden?

Ruiz de Azúa: Wir wollten keinen konkreten Orden darstellen und haben uns deshalb einen Namen ausgedacht. Die Inspiration stammt jedoch von vielen Klausurorden, den typischen spanisch-katholischen Orden.

In einer Szene treffen Maite, die Tante der Hauptfigur Ainara, und die Priorin Isabel aufeinander. Wie sind diese beiden Charaktere angelegt?

Ruiz de Azúa: Es ist wie ein Duell, denn Maite reißt sich sehr zusammen. Sie stößt aber auf eine Mauer, denn diese Institutionen sind für rationale Argumente nicht offen. Maite bringt vernünftige Argumente vor: Das Mädchen ist noch sehr jung. Warum geben wir ihr nicht mehr Zeit? Doch was man für Gottes Willen hält, lässt sich mit rationalen Argumenten nicht infrage stellen. Das macht Toleranz oft so schwierig.

Verkörpert Maite so etwas wie das progressive, aufgeklärte Spanien? Und verliert sie am Ende?

Ruiz de Azúa: Manche werden denken, dass sie verliert. Andere aber, dass sie gewinnt. Maite hat es viel schwerer, denn sie glaubt an keinen Gott und muss sich in der Welt mit ihren eigenen Einschätzungen, Zweifeln und Überzeugungen zurechtfinden. Sie setzt sich mit sehr komplexen Fragen auseinander, als Ainara ihre Entscheidung trifft, von der Maite glaubt, dass sie sie verhindern müsse. Doch am Ende kann sie nur noch ausrasten und ihre Liebe zeigen – allerdings aus einer Position heraus, in der es bereits zu spät ist.

Alle Ihre Filme handeln von der Familie. Was bedeutet Familie für Sie?

Ruiz de Azúa: Die Familie ist eine Keimzelle der Gesellschaft. Sie kann Zuflucht und ein ganz wunderbarer Ort sein, wenn die emotionalen Bindungen gut funktionieren und man einander mit Respekt behandelt. Oft ist das aber nicht der Fall. Darüber zu sprechen, ist ein großes Tabu. Bis heute gilt es als absolutes Tabu, mit der eigenen Familie zu brechen – selbst wenn schmerzhafte Dinge geschehen, wenn jemand emotional vernachlässigt wird oder ähnliches. Wir sind so erzogen worden, dass man nicht mit der Familie bricht, obwohl es manchmal das Gesündeste wäre. Mich interessieren diese unangenehmen Bereiche der Familie – sowohl als Institution als auch als Bezugsgruppe. Manchmal ist sie ein Ort, an dem man sich sicher und verstanden fühlt, der einen im Leben am stärksten geprägt hat. Sie kann aber auch der Ort sein, an dem man den größten Schaden erleidet.

Ihr Film spielt in Innenräumen: im Haus der Familie, im Kloster und auch in der Schule. Inwiefern korrespondiert diese Ästhetik mit der Geschichte?

Ruiz de Azúa: Das Unangenehmste, Beunruhigendste oder Spannendste spielt sich im geschützten privaten Raum ab – und das sind normalerweise Innenräume. Es sind diese Gespräche, die man halb versteckt in einer Küche führt, oder diese Diskussionen am Mittagstisch. Aber auch die ganz persönliche Geschichte einer religiösen Berufung spielt sich in Innenräumen ab, bei Gesprächen in einer vertraulichen Atmosphäre, zwischen einem Erwachsenen und einer Minderjährigen, in denen es um Freunde und ähnliche Dinge geht.

Visuell ist das auch sehr interessant. Ich erzähle von einem Mädchen, das eine Berufung zum Leben in einem Klausurkloster verspürt und sich hinter vier Wände zurückziehen will. Dabei ging es auch um die Vorstellungen von Eingeschlossensein und Klaustrophobie. Auch die Familie kann sehr klaustrophobisch sein. Wir wollten beide Räume einander angleichen – die religiöse Welt und die Familie sind nicht voneinander getrennt.

Die Musik ist sehr wichtig im Film. Wie lief der Entstehungsprozess ab?

Ruiz de Azúa: Ich bin sehr zurückhaltend, wenn es darum geht, Musik einzusetzen. Man kann damit stark beeinflussen, manipulieren oder bestimmte Aspekte übermäßig hervorheben. Musik interessiert mich nur dann, wenn sie eine zusätzliche Ebene oder einen Kontrast schafft. In diesem Fall war es der Chor – eine außerschulische Aktivität, bei der Ainara den Jungen und seine Freunde kennenlernen konnte.

Der Chor war auch in anderer Hinsicht interessant, denn Chormusik hat etwas Spirituelles an sich. Auch wenn sie nicht religiös ist, besitzt sie doch etwas Transzendentes. Es war sehr schön, damit in eher alltäglichen Szenen zu spielen. Meine Protagonistin ist Teenagerin. Was sie besonders macht, ist der Umstand, dass sie etwas Transzendentes oder Spirituelles empfindet, das ihre Freunde nicht spüren. Die Musik war für mich eine Möglichkeit, den Zuschauern dieses Gefühl zu vermitteln.

Ich beginne den Film mit einem Stück von Quevedo, einem nicht nur bei Jugendlichen beliebten Rapper. Bei der ersten Vorführung in San Sebastián kam das Publikum schon in Stimmung, als die Musik einsetzte; die Menschen wollten schon klatschen, während der Vorspann lief. article_text:
Organized by Blue Lotus Gallery to mark the release of the new publication Hong Kong Symphony , the exhibition returns to Fan Ho ’s photographs of Hong Kong and his distinctive way of seeing the city in the 1950s and 1960s. The exhibition coincides with a renewed international focus on Fan Ho’s work, with presentations taking place at major institutions and galleries across Europe and Asia.

Fan Ho’s photographs are among the most recognisable images of post-war Hong Kong. He photographed the city’s streets, markets and harbour fronts with a sharp sense of timing and composition, revealing poetry in everyday life and drama in fleeting moments. His pictures are carefully structured but never static, capturing the density, energy and changing character of a city in transformation. In Fan Ho’s own words: ‘Photography should offer something we cannot see with our eyes but feel with our hearts’, a conviction that lies at the very core of his practice.

The exhibition places Fan Ho’s photographs alongside selected vintage works by other Hong Kong photographers of the same generation, offering a broader perspective of the photographic landscape in which his work emerged. Together, these images reveal different approaches to photographing the city during a period of significant change, while illuminating the wider photographic culture that helped shape its visual identity.

In these works, Hong Kong appears as a place of striking contrasts. We see an older way of life in scenes of rice fields, oxen, hillside farms, and boat communities gathered in harbours thick with smoke from evening cooking fires. At the same time, other photographs show a city in motion: buildings under construction, crowded markets, new roads, and the gradual shift from low-rise streetscapes to a more vertical urban form. Through the eyes of Hong Kong’s salon photographers, this period was not only documented but transformed into images of formal beauty, atmosphere, and quiet poignancy. Today, much of what they recorded has disappeared. For this reason, these photographs are more than artistic achievements: they also form an important visual archive of a Hong Kong that has largely passed from view.

The exhibition is presented alongside the brand-new publication Hong Kong Symphony , which brings together Fan Ho’s photographs of the city in book form.

The release coincides with several international exhibitions featuring his work, including a major solo exhibition at Palazzo Falletti di Barolo in Turin, his inclusion in Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography at Tate Modern in London, and presentations at Fotografiska in Shanghai this fall and Shenzhen next spring.

Together, these exhibitions reflect the growing international visibility of Fan Ho’s work and its place within the wider history of photography.

About Fan Ho: Fan Ho (1931–2016) was a master photographer best known for his black-and-white images of mid-20th-century Hong Kong. Born in Shanghai, he began photography at 14 with a Kodak Brownie given to him by his father, and moved to Hong Kong with his family at 18. There, he explored the city’s streets, alleys, rooftops and harbour fronts, creating much of his most celebrated work before the age of 28.

Fan Ho’s photographs are distinguished by their dramatic use of light and shadow, precise composition, architectural geometry and deep sensitivity to everyday life. Rather than simply documenting Hong Kong’s buildings or monuments, he sought to capture the soul of the city and the resilience of its people. His work is often compared to Henri Cartier-Bresson for its attention to the decisive moment, though Fan Ho’s images carry a more cinematic and atmospheric quality.

Over his career, Fan Ho won nearly 300 local and international awards, published several photography books, and was also active in the film industry as an actor and director. A Fellow of the Royal Photographic Society and the Royal Society of Arts in England, his work is held in major public and private collections, including M+ Museum, Hong Kong Heritage Museum, Bibliothèque nationale de France, San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and Santa Barbara Museum of Art.

article_text:
India’s T-Series has boarded “ The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj ,” Sandeep Singh’s historical epic starring “ Kantara ” actor Rishab Shetty as the Maratha king.

The project will now be made in two parts, and filming begins in early 2027.

Bhushan Kumar and Krishan Kumar will produce for T-Series Films, and Shetty also comes on as a co-producer. To mark the partnership, Bhushan Kumar presented Shetty with a century-old painting of the Maratha ruler.

Related Stories

Shetty wrote, directed and starred in “Kantara,” the 2022 Kannada-language hit that won him the Indian National Film Award for best actor. Its prequel, “Kantara: Chapter 1,” was released in 2025 and grossed more than $91 million worldwide.

Shetty and Singh first announced the film in December 2024 .

Across the two films, the saga will follow Shivaji Maharaj through his major battles and victories, the sacrifices that came with them and episodes from his life that are less widely known. The story centers on his skill as a military strategist, his leadership and his idea of Swarajya.

The production will have a large ensemble cast. Its creative team combines talent from India and abroad.

“Maharashtra and Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj have given us a legacy to be proud of, and I believe it is our responsibility to honor that legacy through cinema and share it with the world,” Bhushan Kumar said. “When Sandeep Singh narrated ‘The Pride of Bharat – Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj,’ I felt a deep sense of responsibility to bring this extraordinary story to the big screen.”

Kumar cited Shetty’s screen presence and his ability to bring legendary figures to life, adding that he believes the team is the right combination “to bring the courage, vision and spirit of Swarajya to audiences across generations. For T-Series, this is more than a film; it is a tribute to Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj and his timeless legacy.”

Shivaji founded the Maratha kingdom in 17th-century western India and spent much of his life fighting the Mughal Empire. He is revered in Maharashtra and a frequent subject for Indian filmmakers. Recent films about him and his circle include “Tanhaji: The Unsung Warrior” (2020), the Marathi film “Har Har Mahadev” (2022) and “Chhaava” (2025), which centered on his son Sambhaji. In May, Riteish Deshmukh directed “Raja Shivaji” and starred in it as the king. Released in the Hindi and Marathi languages, it became the highest-grossing Marathi film of all time.

Pre-production is under way ahead of the 2027 shoot.

Singh co-wrote the film with Rishi Virmani. Gulshan Kumar and T-Series Films present the project, which Legend Studios produces alongside T-Series Films. Shiv Chanana and Kabiir Sadanand join Shetty as co-producers.

article_text:
From Sunday church attire to contemporary fashion, ‘Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style’ at the Art Gallery of Ontario explores how clothing has shaped Black identity, cultural expression and self-determination across generations.

Can getting dressed become a declaration of identity, resistance, and belonging?

In ‘Sunday Best: The Power & The Glory of Black Style ’ , the Art Gallery of Ontario examines the cultural and political significance of fashion within Black diasporic communities, tracing histories of migration, activism and self-expression from the 1880s to the present.

Bringing together fashion, visual art, archival materials and time-based media, the exhibition considers how clothing has served as a powerful language through which Black communities have asserted dignity, celebrated individuality and challenged systems of racial exclusion. At its centre is the enduring tradition of dressing in one’s finest attire, a practice that extends beyond aesthetics to encompass cultural pride, collective memory and the politics of visibility.

Conceived and curated by Dr Julie Crooks and Dr Jason Cyrus, alongside Amanda Bock and Clare Sauro, the exhibition makes its world debut in Toronto. Moving between historical and contemporary expressions of Black style, ‘Sunday Best ’ reveals how fashion operates as both personal expression and collective statement, inviting audiences to reconsider the relationship between appearance, agency and the ongoing struggle for self-representation.

This exhibition is on view at the Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto until 28 February 2027.

[{"type": "paragraph", "text": "If you spend much time in the American West, the indelible traces of mining are impossible to miss. From abandoned shafts and ghost towns to gleaming refineries and places newly resplendent with fancy houses and fancier pickup trucks, the perennial boom-and-bust shapes the landscape. In Butte or the Bakken Formation, northern Utah or the Navajo Nation, it is clear that American history is a procession of resources being wrested from lodes far beneath the surface, its modernity a great speculative venture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photography’s history, too, is a mineral one. As a spate of recent ecologically minded scholarship reminds us, the act of recording photonic energy is metallurgy in miniature: precious amalgams activated by other chemicals affixed to copper or tin. The rise of photography in the 1840s was made possible by new strikes of silver and gold. And many of those early camera operators set their lenses on those doing the sluicing, digging, and refining. Timothy H. O’Sullivan was famous for his battlefield images and harsh framing of the West’s Rocky Mountains, but he was also among the first to document the rush towns of Nevada that cropped up after the Comstock Lode was found in the territory in 1859. From the beginning, American practitioners worked to forge new genres of portraiture and landscape photography centered around these pockets of extraction."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/262MAG798_OSullivan_HR.jpg", "alt": "Timothy H. Emerging from ecological humanities and theories of the Anthropocene over the past decade, it can now mean anything exploitative or inequitable, especially in economic relations. In mining history, the term simply describes the laborious—often brutal—process of moving matter from one place to another, converting it from its rawer forms into more refined yields. Extracting is something humans have done all over the world for millennia, and it was the key driver of many of the colonial endeavors that transformed the planet since the fifteenth century. Visualizing such a sprawling terrain is an elusive task, but one to which photography’s relentless archival bent is well suited. Accordingly, the exhibition Beneath the Surface: Mining and American Photography , which opened a multi-city tour this May at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, and this October at the Milwaukee Art Museum , draws together some 150 works and makes explicit an undercurrent running through the medium’s nearly two-hundred-year trajectory.", "links": [{"text": "National Gallery of Art", "url": "https://www.nga.gov/exhibitions/beneath-surface-mining-american-photography"}, {"text": "Milwaukee Art Museum", "url": "https://mam.org/exhibitions/beneath-the-surface/"}]}, {"type": "quote", "text": "From the beginning, American photographers created genres centered around pockets of extraction."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Marshaling such a vast range of objects could have been a task without end, spanning the gamut of countless corporate, popular, and fine-art photographs. Based on my conversations with the curators, Diane Waggoner and Kristen Gaylord, Beneath the Surface is a trenchant exhibition—one that shows American mining as not just a Western story but one that crisscrosses the United States, not merely a curiosity of a subset of photographers but a leitmotif visible in unexpected places. According to Waggoner and Gaylord, this focus allows viewers to newly “understand photography as a central tool in both depicting and critiquing the industries that enable our contemporary world, and to help us all better understand how photographers have deployed it throughout the medium’s history.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026_Aperture264_1600x900_Fan_gray-copy.jpg", "alt": "Aperture Magazine Subscription", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Aperture Magazine Subscription"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Much recent writing on photography and mining focuses on the connections between extractive industries and colonialism, stretching back to the Iberian quests across the Atlantic in search of precious metals and up to our current moment. Even now, a scramble is on for rare earth metals to power our cars, microchips, and military technology. Versions of this story wend through Beneath the Surface , as in several works by the Diné artist Will Wilson that adapt the surveillant mode of the aerial image to reveal the insidious cycle of a colonial paradigm that persists out West: the speculation of new minerals on Indigenous land, the abandonment of those who live there, and the depredations of the waste left behind. His Shiprock Disposal Site, Shiprock, Navajo Nation, 36 (2020) foregrounds a sprawling pentagonal complex in New Mexico that one might mistake for a Michael Heizer earthwork. Off in the distance, storm clouds dapple a high desert sunset near the titular Tsé Bit’a’í (the Navajo name for Shiprock), a rock monolith of cosmological significance to the Diné. In this way, Wilson juxtaposes two kinds of mapping—the ruthless abstraction of the surveyors’ grid and the emplaced topographies of the people on the ground."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/262MAG840_Wilson_HR.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/262MAG839_Maisel_HR_1.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tens of millions of tons of uranium were cleaved from Indigenous land during the twentieth century, used to make warheads, reactors (J. Robert Oppenheimer built his bomb just a few hours away), and X-ray photography. The disposal site contains the radioactive residues of that process. New Mexico is honeycombed in this way, with deep caverns from which ore was taken, and others in which its dangerous by-products are entombed. Just hidden from view in Wilson’s landscape is the San Juan River, a fragile lifeline in this arid region."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Still, photographers have long known that a perverse beauty persists in such instrumental images; even the chemistry of toxicity has its chromatic appeal. This is especially true in the hands of David Maisel, whose interplay of the photographic and painterly has long sought to chart the tailings and holding ponds left in the wake of mining industries. Gold processing, for instance, relies on cyanide and sulfuric acid treatments, and yields contaminated wastewater, laden with heavy metals that pollute the surrounding ecosystem. Maisel notes the asymmetry, that “the word pond connotes something idyllic, perhaps a site where Thoreau might reflect on the natural world. . . . But no human-made tailings pond is wholly impervious to failure; they are essentially earthen dams.” His American Mine (Carlin, Nevada 1) (2007) depicts such a pond, which seeps across the frame in what Maisel calls a cyanide-infused “lurid green.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "For both Wilson and Maisel, this tension between the aesthetic allure and political-economic critique captured in their work needn’t be resolved. Describing his depictions of Nevada’s Carlin gold district, Maisel told me, “We may be seduced by its beauty and then feel a sense of betrayal when we comprehend the darkness of its subject. article_text:
If you spend much time in the American West, the indelible traces of mining are impossible to miss. From abandoned shafts and ghost towns to gleaming refineries and places newly resplendent with fancy houses and fancier pickup trucks, the perennial boom-and-bust shapes the landscape. In Butte or the Bakken Formation, northern Utah or the Navajo Nation, it is clear that American history is a procession of resources being wrested from lodes far beneath the surface, its modernity a great speculative venture.

Photography’s history, too, is a mineral one. As a spate of recent ecologically minded scholarship reminds us, the act of recording photonic energy is metallurgy in miniature: precious amalgams activated by other chemicals affixed to copper or tin. The rise of photography in the 1840s was made possible by new strikes of silver and gold. And many of those early camera operators set their lenses on those doing the sluicing, digging, and refining. Timothy H. O’Sullivan was famous for his battlefield images and harsh framing of the West’s Rocky Mountains, but he was also among the first to document the rush towns of Nevada that cropped up after the Comstock Lode was found in the territory in 1859. From the beginning, American practitioners worked to forge new genres of portraiture and landscape photography centered around these pockets of extraction.

Today, extraction is a buzzword. Emerging from ecological humanities and theories of the Anthropocene over the past decade, it can now mean anything exploitative or inequitable, especially in economic relations. In mining history, the term simply describes the laborious—often brutal—process of moving matter from one place to another, converting it from its rawer forms into more refined yields. Extracting is something humans have done all over the world for millennia, and it was the key driver of many of the colonial endeavors that transformed the planet since the fifteenth century. Visualizing such a sprawling terrain is an elusive task, but one to which photography’s relentless archival bent is well suited. Accordingly, the exhibition Beneath the Surface: Mining and American Photography , which opened a multi-city tour this May at the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, and this October at the Milwaukee Art Museum , draws together some 150 works and makes explicit an undercurrent running through the medium’s nearly two-hundred-year trajectory.

From the beginning, American photographers created genres centered around pockets of extraction.

Marshaling such a vast range of objects could have been a task without end, spanning the gamut of countless corporate, popular, and fine-art photographs. Based on my conversations with the curators, Diane Waggoner and Kristen Gaylord, Beneath the Surface is a trenchant exhibition—one that shows American mining as not just a Western story but one that crisscrosses the United States, not merely a curiosity of a subset of photographers but a leitmotif visible in unexpected places. According to Waggoner and Gaylord, this focus allows viewers to newly “understand photography as a central tool in both depicting and critiquing the industries that enable our contemporary world, and to help us all better understand how photographers have deployed it throughout the medium’s history.”

Much recent writing on photography and mining focuses on the connections between extractive industries and colonialism, stretching back to the Iberian quests across the Atlantic in search of precious metals and up to our current moment. Even now, a scramble is on for rare earth metals to power our cars, microchips, and military technology. Versions of this story wend through Beneath the Surface , as in several works by the Diné artist Will Wilson that adapt the surveillant mode of the aerial image to reveal the insidious cycle of a colonial paradigm that persists out West: the speculation of new minerals on Indigenous land, the abandonment of those who live there, and the depredations of the waste left behind. His Shiprock Disposal Site, Shiprock, Navajo Nation, 36 (2020) foregrounds a sprawling pentagonal complex in New Mexico that one might mistake for a Michael Heizer earthwork. Off in the distance, storm clouds dapple a high desert sunset near the titular Tsé Bit’a’í (the Navajo name for Shiprock), a rock monolith of cosmological significance to the Diné. In this way, Wilson juxtaposes two kinds of mapping—the ruthless abstraction of the surveyors’ grid and the emplaced topographies of the people on the ground.

Tens of millions of tons of uranium were cleaved from Indigenous land during the twentieth century, used to make warheads, reactors (J. Robert Oppenheimer built his bomb just a few hours away), and X-ray photography. The disposal site contains the radioactive residues of that process. New Mexico is honeycombed in this way, with deep caverns from which ore was taken, and others in which its dangerous by-products are entombed. Just hidden from view in Wilson’s landscape is the San Juan River, a fragile lifeline in this arid region.

Still, photographers have long known that a perverse beauty persists in such instrumental images; even the chemistry of toxicity has its chromatic appeal. This is especially true in the hands of David Maisel, whose interplay of the photographic and painterly has long sought to chart the tailings and holding ponds left in the wake of mining industries. Gold processing, for instance, relies on cyanide and sulfuric acid treatments, and yields contaminated wastewater, laden with heavy metals that pollute the surrounding ecosystem. Maisel notes the asymmetry, that “the word pond connotes something idyllic, perhaps a site where Thoreau might reflect on the natural world. . . . But no human-made tailings pond is wholly impervious to failure; they are essentially earthen dams.” His American Mine (Carlin, Nevada 1) (2007) depicts such a pond, which seeps across the frame in what Maisel calls a cyanide-infused “lurid green.”

For both Wilson and Maisel, this tension between the aesthetic allure and political-economic critique captured in their work needn’t be resolved. Describing his depictions of Nevada’s Carlin gold district, Maisel told me, “We may be seduced by its beauty and then feel a sense of betrayal when we comprehend the darkness of its subject. I like that contradiction, that ricochet between beauty and horror, seduction and betrayal.” And given their siting in desert basins removed from most Americans’ daily lives, this sort of mapping is all the more urgent. At the same time, the products and wealth generated by those sites suffuse every facet of our financial system and built environment. This is one reason LaToya Ruby Frazier’s many series foregrounding the rust belt back East continue to resonate—because they show us the dense social worlds emanating from the more familiar landscapes of the mill, foundry, or factory.

Frazier was raised in Braddock, Pennsylvania, where Appalachian coal country converges with the industrial imperium of the early twentieth century. This Pittsburgh region was built on steel, a beacon for a new middle class and Black families on the Great Migration. But by the time of Frazier’s childhood, in the 1980s, much of the US Steel plant and its jobs were gone, while the toxicity remained. She and her family were left to contend with a contemporary ghost town, where even the local medical center closed its doors, leaving the borough to the vagaries of foreclosure or gentrification. One of several Frazier photographs in Beneath the Surface is drawn from her celebrated photo-essay of domestic interiors. Another shows the Monongahela River arcing picturesquely around two remaining operational furnaces, interlaced by highway and railcars: The black-and-white scene was taken in 2013 but could be a postcard from another era, in which such vernacular architecture manifested the mined world in human terms.

For all the power of these industrial topographies, Frazier is best known as a portraitist of the American working class. In this way, her immersive projects are of a piece with journalistic forebears such as Gordon Parks and Margaret Bourke-White (both featured in the show, with their entrancing geometries of oil pipelines and poured molten ore, respectively). Yet Frazier’s contemporary icons breathe in new ways in Beneath the Surface when seen alongside a host of anonymous mine workers captured in the antique tonalities of the nineteenth century. While extractive capitalism is the structure in which modern mining unfolds, that same mining is done by the countless humans toiling at the ore face. This has always been rough labor conducted at excruciating temperatures in the stygian depths. There is a reason that mine head frames (which hoist people, animals, and ore up and down their cableways) are called “gallows”: Drowning, explosion, asphyxiation, and tunnel collapse have always been present dangers; deafness, silicosis, black lung, and other maladies stalk those workers years later.

Beneath the Surface ’s task, then, is to strike a difficult balance, telling a story of extraction from its widest conceptual angles while grounding it in the human tableaux in which involute systems are animated. It is an important time to revisit this American story, not only because versions of it are playing out around the world right now but also because we are still navigating the contradictions and residues of a modernity hewn from the mines. Photography, it is clear, has long drawn our focus to the stakes of that modernity: It’s there in what and how we consume, where we prospect anew, and in the forms of solidarity we seek. Just because what happens beneath the surface so easily eludes our vision does not mean it does not reverberate up here in the light.

泉太郎

50 秒 Vol.2 soda, 京都 グループ展｜2026年10月10日–12日, 17日–19日

この度、 泉太郎 は京都のアーティスト・ラン・スペースsodaで開催されるグループ展、「 50 秒 Vol.2 」に参加いたします。

2022年に開催された「50秒」展から約4年を経て、「50秒 Vol.2」として新たに2名のゲストキュレーターと34 名のアーティストを迎えて開催される本展は、10月10日(土)、11日（日）、12日（月）、17日（土）、18日 (日)、19（月）の6日間、各アーティストによる50秒の映像作品を展示する展覧会です。

ぜひこの機会にご高覧くださいませ。

10月9日より、 OVERCOAT TOKYOの旗艦店にてOVERCOAT Fall Winter 2026のポップアップイベントが開催される。 会期中は、 今シーズンのルックブックの舞台となったNYの非営利の写真出版社・文化団体『Aperture』と関係の深いアーティスト4名の作品が店内に展示される。このコラボレーションは、『Aperture』現編集長のマイケル・ファミゲッティとデザイナー大丸隆平がNY渡米時からの旧友であり、出会いから約20年の時を経て実現したものだ。

さらに、会期初日とその翌日には、デザイナー大丸とのパーソナルセッションが予定されている。セッションに参加すれば、今回OVERCOATが提示するFWコレクションにより深く 触れられるだろう。Fall Winter 2026のフルコレクションとともに、OVERCOATとApertureが描く空間とビジュアルの世界を、実際の店頭に赴いて堪能したい。秋の深まるこの季節ぜひ出掛けてみたい。

A review by Nkgopoleng Moloi on the 29th of June 2026. This should take you 4 minutes to read.

blank projects 28.05 - 04.07.2026

‘Photography changes our awareness of beauty and hope’ – Robert Adams

In his latest solo exhibition at blank in Cape Town, Thembinkosi Hlatshwayo offers us fragments of a family biography through images that speak to memories of his father, who has since passed. In another sense, the exhibition offers a rethinking of how photography can be rendered and interacted with. Pigment ink on rags and paper reflects a complexity in what images and stories, materials are able to hold. His way of handling material produces a visceral quality that pierces directly at what we see and what we remember. And somehow everything is fragile, obscured, unknowable.

The work I first became familiar with, ‘Slaghuis’, at times very difficult to look at due to its unflinching confrontation with violence, placed the artist squarely in my mind as someone in the business of showing the gritty… He was not trying to soften or coat anything, just show things exactly as they are. And yet even within that brutal work, there was a kind of ethics of care – an aesthetic that did not render the brutal as inhumane. In ‘Song 1: To be left behind’, Hlatshwayo is even more contemplative, evidently, not only regarding the construction of personal histories through imagery but also of the process of constructing the image itself. To be incredibly dull and obvious about it, his medium is the message.

Writing on the medium, curator and author Marvin Heiferman noted that ‘photography, in all its forms and guises, has been notoriously difficult to assess.’ This difficulty, what we might call stickiness , is precisely what I find interesting in Hlatshwayo’s show and his practice. I’m drawn to how he continues to innovate within the medium, turning it around, breaking things and piecing them back together – with some parts missing.

Thembinkosi Hlatshwayo, Bulelwa (2024). Pigment inks on cotton rag 310gsm, 28 x 32 x 3.5 cm (framed)

Through his fractured approach – a partial figure mid motion, serialised self portraits, and what is that? Toes partially veiled? – Hlatshwayo seems to be poking holes in the adage that we need to see more to know more . He seems to be suggesting that there are, in fact, times when the whole (the full picture, as it were) is less than the sum of its parts. It is interesting too to trace his shifting mood through how he chooses to title the work- ‘ I dreamt of a greying world ’ – speaking to fading hopes in a difficult world, ‘ Young Father ’ and ‘ Inkumbulo ’ [memory], perhaps evoking ideas of lineage and survival, set against much more cynical feelings; ‘ The Void ’, ‘ Taking a piss ’ and ‘ Sobaleka ’ [we will run]. Throughout the show, what echoes is the conversation with his father, or more broadly, the figure of the father.

If Louise Bourgeois was obsessive about the mother, as indispensable and useful as a spider, Hlatshwayo hints at the father as an unstable symbol… through grief, loss and the potential for restoration. For me, part of the title ‘To be left behind’ suggests a kind of passivity or at least a sense of accepting a state of circumstances without resistance. By choice, fate, the choice of Gods… death, the father is rendered absent, and painfully, one is left behind. What Hlatswayo can do then is to memorialise. He takes self-portraits (a stand-in image of his father), multiples them and stretches them across the wall as a collaged memorial. The result is unsettling, evoking feelings of death itself. Unsettling and almost beautiful. I say almost because to be fully and perfectly beautiful would be to resist the potential for rupture, which is a necessary condition for creation… for life.

Thembinkosi Hlatshwayo, ‘Song 1- To be left behind ‘(2026). Installation view at blank projects, Cape Town

Through its poeticism and subtle hints, ‘Song 1: To be left behind’ reminds us of the possibility of expanding our consciousness by taking in the reality of others. Hlatshwayo, himself a father, wrestles with his being by reflecting on his father’s life. We, in turn, can reflect on our being through the faces, torsos, toes and tiny objects from his life. We see the image and imagine the emotional state that led to its creation.

As he moves across different forms of experimentation, what remains consistent in Thembinkosi Hlatshwayo’s practice is the feeling of trying to figure (some)thing(s) out. Perhaps he is trying to figure out the truth between the image and experience. Between the personal and the universal. Between the sacrosanct and the mundane. When I look at his work, at particular moments, what I am trying to figure out is the relationship between beauty and hope.

Thembinkosi Hlatshwayo, ‘Song 1- To be left behind’ (2026). Installation view at blank projects, Cape Town

Daily Newsletter

Raven Chacon’s Echoes on Park Avenue

The Pulitzer Prize-winning Diné artist on latest projects, art in NYC for Indigenous Peoples’ Day, and a Felix Gonzalez-Torres show misses the mark.

It’s a beautiful Monday to celebrate Indigenous Peoples’ Day, no matter what the federal government says. In a conversation with Associate Editor Phillip Pyle, Diné musician Raven Chacon discusses his recent improvised performances at the Park Avenue Armory, the “collision” at the heart of all music, and reclaiming the technologies of colonial violence through sound.

Read on for a guide to shows centering Native art around New York City — including Shelley Niro and Sarah Sense, two of my favorite artists — and a critique of a Felix Gonzalez-Torres exhibition that bizarrely glosses over the late artist’s AIDS advocacy and political spirit.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Raven Chacon Sounds the History of the Land

On Wednesday and Thursday night, sound mixers, synthesizers, pedals, speakers, whistles, a turkey call, and a ceramic horn sat on a table at the center of the Veterans Room in Manhattan’s Park Avenue Armory. Serving as the stage for Raven Chacon’s hour-long improvisation sessions for the Armory’s Artists Studio series, the table also offered audiences the rare opportunity to see the prolific artist at play. | Phillip Pyle
